section.title: The Prologue and the Birth of John Foretold
section.sectionRationale: Luke opens his Gospel twice over: first with a formal preface explaining why he writes, then with the scene that begins the story. A careful historian dedicates his orderly account to Theophilus so that he may know the certainty of what he has been taught. Then the curtain rises in the temple, where an aging, childless priest named Zechariah meets the angel Gabriel and hears that his prayers are answered: a son will be born who will go before the Lord in the spirit of Elijah. It is one movement, the writer's purpose and the first act of fulfillment.
section.thesis: Luke writes so that his reader may know the certainty of the gospel, and he begins that gospel where Israel's long silence breaks: in the temple, God answers an old couple's prayer and sends the forerunner who will prepare a people for the Lord.
section.frameNote: Six beats: the orderly account for Theophilus; a righteous, childless couple; Gabriel at the altar of incense; the promise of John; Zechariah's doubt and silence; and Elizabeth's hidden joy.

units.label: The orderly account for Theophilus
units.note: so that you may know the certainty

verses.text: Many have undertaken to compose an account of the things that have been fulfilled among us,
just as they were handed down to us by the initial eyewitnesses and servants of the word.
Therefore, having carefully investigated everything from the beginning, it seemed good also to me to write an {{kathexes|orderly}} account for you, most excellent Theophilus,
so that you may know the {{asphaleia|certainty}} of the things you have been taught.

units.label: A righteous, childless couple
units.note: no children, well along in years

verses.text: In the time of Herod king of Judea there was a priest named Zechariah, who belonged to the priestly division of Abijah, and whose wife Elizabeth was a descendant of Aaron.
Both of them were righteous in the sight of God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and decrees of the Lord.
But they had no children, because Elizabeth was barren, and they were both well along in years.

units.label: Gabriel at the altar of incense

verses.text: One day while Zechariah’s division was on duty and he was serving as priest before God,
he was chosen by lot, according to the custom of the priesthood, to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense.
And at the hour of the incense offering, the whole congregation was praying outside.
Just then an angel of the Lord appeared to Zechariah, standing at the right side of the altar of incense.
When Zechariah saw him, he was startled and gripped with fear.

units.label: The promise of John
units.note: in the spirit and power of Elijah

verses.text: But the angel said to him, “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, because your prayer has been heard. Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you are to give him the name John.
He will be a joy and delight to you, and many will rejoice at his birth,
for he will be great in the sight of the Lord. He shall never take wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the {{pneuma|Holy Spirit}} even from his mother’s womb.
Many of the sons of Israel he will turn back to the Lord their God.

And he will go on before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to their children and the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous, to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.”

units.label: Zechariah's doubt and silence
units.note: you will be silent until the day this comes to pass

verses.text: “How can I be sure of this?” Zechariah asked the angel. “I am an old man, and my wife is well along in years.”
“I am Gabriel,” replied the angel. “I stand in the presence of God, and I have been sent to speak to you and to bring you this {{euangelizo|good news}}.
And now you will be silent and unable to speak until the day this comes to pass, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled at their proper time.”
Meanwhile, the people were waiting for Zechariah and wondering why he took so long in the temple.
When he came out and was unable to speak to them, they realized he had seen a vision in the temple. He kept making signs to them but remained unable to speak.
And when the days of his service were complete, he returned home.

units.label: Elizabeth's hidden joy
units.note: the Lord has taken away my disgrace

verses.text: After these days, his wife Elizabeth became pregnant and for five months remained in seclusion. She declared,
“The Lord has done this for me. In these days He has shown me favor and taken away my disgrace among the people.”

kathexes.gloss: In order, in sequence, one after another. Luke says he will write an orderly account. He is not claiming a bare chronology so much as a coherent, well-arranged telling that lets the reader see how the pieces fit and where the story is going, from the temple to the empty tomb.

asphaleia.gloss: Certainty, security, firm and unshakable footing. It is the last word of the preface in the Greek and the goal of the whole Gospel: Theophilus, and every reader, may know that the things he has been taught are solid ground, not rumor.

pneuma.gloss: Spirit, breath, wind. Here the Holy Spirit, who fills John even in the womb. Luke's Gospel and its sequel, Acts, are marked by the Spirit at every turn, coming upon the humble to prepare and empower them for God's work.

euangelizo.gloss: To announce good news, to proclaim glad tidings. Gabriel brings good news to Zechariah, and the same word runs through Luke: to the shepherds, to the poor, and out to the nations. The Gospel of joy begins with an angel's announcement in the temple.

basic.context: Luke begins with a short preface, unusual among the Gospels, telling us he has carefully investigated everything and is writing an orderly account for a man named Theophilus so that he may be sure of what he has been taught. Then the story proper opens in the temple. Zechariah, an old priest, and his wife Elizabeth are righteous but childless, a grief in their world. While Zechariah offers incense, the angel Gabriel tells him his prayer is answered: a son, John, will be born who will go before the Lord in the spirit of Elijah. Zechariah doubts, and is struck silent until it comes true. Elizabeth conceives and rejoices that God has taken away her disgrace.
basic.hermeneutics: The first four verses tell us how to read the whole book: as a careful, truthful account meant to give assurance, not a collection of legends. From verse 5 the narrative unfolds in the style of Old Testament birth stories, so that we hear echoes of Abraham and Sarah, of Hannah, of the barren who are given a child by God. The key questions are simple: why does Luke write, and what is God doing when He breaks four centuries of prophetic silence to answer an old couple's prayer?
basic.originalLanguages: Luke promises an orderly account, kathexes, so that Theophilus may know the certainty, asphaleia, of what he has learned. Gabriel brings good news, the verb euangelizo that will echo through the Gospel, and the child will be filled with the pneuma, the Holy Spirit, from the womb.
basic.typology: John comes in the spirit and power of Elijah, fulfilling the promise that Elijah would come before the great day of the Lord. The barren womb opened by God recalls Sarah, Rebekah, and Hannah, and points to the God who gives life where there is none, ultimately at the virgin's womb and the empty tomb.
basic.christ: This chapter is all preparation for Christ. John is not the light but the one who goes before the Lord to make ready a people for Him. Every promise here leans forward to Jesus, the Lord whose way John will prepare.
basic.god: God is the one who keeps His word across long silence, who hears prayer, who remembers the humble and the barren, and who works through ordinary faithful people like Zechariah and Elizabeth. He is gracious even in the discipline of Zechariah's silence.
basic.crossReferences: Malachi 4 promises Elijah before the day of the Lord. 1 Samuel 1 tells of Hannah, another woman given a son by God. Genesis 18 recounts the promise to aged Abraham and Sarah. And Acts 1 shows Luke's second volume, addressed again to Theophilus.
basic.oneStory: After centuries of waiting, God moves again. He answers prayer, opens a barren womb, and sends the forerunner, so that the whole Gospel can begin with the note that will never leave it: God is keeping His promises, and joy is coming.

context.literary:
Luke 1:1-4 is a single long, balanced sentence in Greek, the kind of formal preface that Greek and Jewish historians put at the front of their works. Then, at verse 5, the style changes completely. The polished Greek gives way to Greek that sounds like the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament, with its simple 'and it came to pass' rhythm. Luke is signalling that the story he is about to tell is the next chapter of the one the Old Testament has been telling.

The passage is built as the first half of a pair. Luke sets the announcement to Zechariah, 1:5-25, beside the announcement to Mary, 1:26-38, so that each is a mirror of the other. Both open with an angel, a fear, 'Do not be afraid,' a promised son, a name given from heaven, a description of the son's future, an objection, and a sign. The details differ at every point where John is lesser and Jesus greater, and a careful reader keeps the two side by side.

Within the first half, there is a deliberate movement from earth to heaven and back. The scene opens with Herod king of Judea, 1:5, and ends with a woman in seclusion, 1:24. In between everything happens in or around the temple, and the temple itself is the setting for the end of one age. The whole congregation is outside praying, 1:10, the priest alone is inside, and the angel stands at the right of the altar of incense.

Notice also the way the narrator slows down the clock. The silence of Zechariah stretches the temple scene, with the people waiting and wondering at the delay, 1:21. When he comes out unable to speak, the narrative itself suspends: the sign that something has happened is the speechless priest. The silence ends only at John's naming, 1:64, which is the other end of the pair.
context.historical:
Luke dates the story 'in the time of Herod king of Judea,' 1:5, so before 4 BC, when Herod the Great died. Judea was under a client king who ruled by Roman favour, and the temple he had rebuilt was grand, but the people lived under foreign power and suspected rulers. It had been about four centuries since the last of the Old Testament prophets, and many in Israel read their moment as a time of waiting.

The priesthood was divided into twenty-four divisions, each serving a week in the temple twice a year, with the great festivals all together. David had arranged them, and the eighth lot fell to Abijah, 1 Chronicles 24:10, which is Zechariah's division. A priest who offered the incense in the Holy Place was chosen by lot, verse 9, and for many priests that was a once in a lifetime honour. The incense was burned morning and evening beside the altar that stood just in front of the veil, while the people prayed outside, verse 10. Prayer was linked with incense in Israel's worship, as in Psalm 141:2.

Childlessness carried a heavy burden. Old Testament stories treat the barren woman as one who is in need of God's remembrance, as with Sarah, Rachel and Hannah. Elizabeth speaks of her 'disgrace among the people,' verse 25, and Rachel had said almost the same thing, Genesis 30:22-23. Yet Luke insists that they were not barren because they were sinners. They were 'righteous in the sight of God, walking blamelessly,' verse 6, a statement that shuts the door on any assumption that suffering is a measure of guilt.

The dedication of the book, to 'most excellent Theophilus,' reflects ancient practice. That title is used elsewhere of Roman governors, Felix and Festus, Acts 23:26 and 26:25, which suggests Theophilus was a person of rank, perhaps a patron who funded the work, or at least a believer of standing. The book is written to be read aloud in churches and passed to a wider reader.
context.canonical:
The start of Luke resumes the Old Testament story on a note it had left unfinished. Malachi, the last book of the Old Testament, ends with two promises: that the Lord would send a messenger to prepare the way before Him, Malachi 3:1, and that He would send Elijah before the great day of the LORD, 'to turn the hearts of the fathers to their children,' Malachi 4:5-6. Gabriel's words to Zechariah in verses 16 and 17 pick up the language of the second promise, and the BSB footnote at 1:17 sends the reader to Malachi 4:5-6.

The angel himself carries a history. Gabriel appeared to Daniel to explain visions, Daniel 8:16, and to give him understanding in answer to his prayer 'about the time of the evening sacrifice,' Daniel 9:21-23. Now he appears at the hour of the incense and again an answer to prayer comes. Daniel had been told of seventy weeks, and Luke's readers are meant to feel that the time Daniel waited for is arriving.

The birth stories of Genesis, Judges and Samuel stand behind the scene. Sarah laughed in doubt and God asked, 'Is anything too difficult for the LORD?' Genesis 18:11-14. Manoah's wife was barren, an angel promised a son who would never take strong drink and would begin to deliver Israel, Judges 13:2-5. Hannah prayed and 'the LORD remembered her,' 1 Samuel 1:19-20. Luke places Elizabeth among these women.

The reading continues forward. John's preaching in Luke 3:3-6 is introduced with Isaiah 40:3-5, 'Prepare the way for the LORD,' where Luke has 'the Lord.' Jesus says that John is the Elijah who was to come, Matthew 11:14, though John himself, asked directly, says 'I am not,' John 1:21. Luke's second volume opens by looking back to this one and addressing the same Theophilus, Acts 1:1.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke tells Theophilus exactly why he wrote: so that he 'may know the certainty of the things you have been taught,' 1:4. That is a pastoral purpose before it is a historical one. A believer who had heard the faith from others, perhaps in an atmosphere of doubt or rumour, is given a carefully ordered account to rest on. Luke does not hide that others have written before him, nor that he drew on what 'the initial eyewitnesses and servants of the word' handed down, 1:2. He presents himself as a researcher who has traced everything from the beginning.

Within the story, Luke wants the reader to see that God's way of beginning is quiet and costly. The new age begins not with a triumph but with an elderly couple, a priest no one would have noticed, and a prayer answered long after it was prayed. The prayer of verse 13 is not only for a child. Spoken in the temple at the hour of incense, it may also echo the longing of the whole people, and the answer is bigger than Zechariah supposed.

Luke wants us to hear the warning in Zechariah's silence as well. A righteous man, standing in the presence of an angel, has Scripture's own example in front of him, and still asks 'How can I be sure of this?' The sign he asks for is given as a rebuke. Luke does this so that the quiet trust of Mary and Elizabeth, in the verses that follow, will stand out against it.

He also wants the readers to understand that John is a witness and a servant, not a rival. Everything said of him, great as it is, points past him to 'the Lord' whose way he prepares.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes what happened to one old priest and his wife, and Gabriel's promises are given to them, not to every childless couple. A reader should be careful here. The story shows that God hears prayer and keeps His promises, but it does not guarantee that each long prayer will be answered in the way we ask. Many equally faithful people have waited and not received a child. What carries forward is the character of the God who remembers, not a formula for getting what we want.

Zechariah's silence is likewise a record, not a rule. He asked for a sign and received one, and Luke does not say that every doubt is punished by a lost voice. Mary asks 'How can this be?' a few verses later, and she is not rebuked, because her question is about method while his was about reliability. The difference is in the heart behind the question, and it is a reminder that God can tell honest asking from unbelief.

The preface is something Christians can take directly. Luke commends investigation, orderly study and careful witness as honourable ways of serving the faith. The believer is not asked to trust blindly or to put aside questions, but to look at the evidence that has been gathered and to find in it certainty, asphaleia, in the things taught.

debates.question: Why is Zechariah struck silent when Mary, who asks a similar question, is not?

views.label: His question expressed unbelief; hers sought understanding
views.case: Zechariah says 'How can I be sure of this?' and points to his and his wife's age, verse 18, as though God's word needed more evidence. Gabriel's reply is that he 'did not believe my words,' verse 20. Mary asks 'How can this be, since I am a virgin?' Luke 1:34, and is told how, and answers 'I am the Lord's servant,' 1:38. Elizabeth later praises Mary as the one who 'believed,' 1:45.

views.label: The difference lies in the circumstances, not the heart
views.case: Some think the two questions are less different than they look and that the contrast is mainly literary. Zechariah, a priest steeped in the stories of Abraham and Sarah, ought to have remembered that God had done this before. Mary had no precedent for a virgin conception, so her question is more naturally one of how.

views.label: The silence is a sign and a mercy as well as a discipline
views.case: Gabriel says Zechariah will be silent 'until the day this comes to pass,' verse 20, which makes it a sign of the promise itself. The silence gives the people outside evidence that a vision occurred, verse 22, and gives Zechariah nine months to learn to trust. His first words afterward are praise, 1:64.

debates.bearing: All three can be held together. The text calls the silence a response to unbelief, but it also functions as a sign and ends in blessing, and the contrast with Mary shows that God welcomes honest questions asked in faith while exposing a doubt that asks Him to prove Himself.

debates.question: Is John the Elijah who was to come, or not?

views.label: John is the promised Elijah
views.case: Gabriel says John will go before the Lord 'in the spirit and power of Elijah,' verse 17, quoting the language of Malachi 4:5-6, and Jesus says plainly, 'he is the Elijah who was to come,' Matthew 11:14. Luke's account makes John the fulfilment of Malachi's promise.

views.label: Another Elijah is still to come
views.case: John himself answers, 'I am not,' when asked if he is Elijah, John 1:21, and some conclude that Malachi's prophecy is only partially fulfilled in John and will have a final fulfilment at the end. The mountain of transfiguration includes Elijah himself, Mark 9:4.

views.label: John is Elijah in function, not in person
views.case: The angel's words are carefully chosen: 'in the spirit and power of Elijah,' not Elijah himself. John denies being Elijah returned in person, while Jesus says he fills Elijah's role. Both statements are true.

debates.bearing: Luke's wording supports the third view and so reconciles the apparent conflict. John does Elijah's work of calling a people back before the Lord comes, and he does it in Elijah's power, without being the man himself.

study.originalLanguages:
Luke's opening word list is that of a historian. He says many have undertaken to compose an account, the Greek diegesis, a narrative that sets events in sequence. He says the matters have been 'fulfilled among us,' from a verb, plerophoreo, that carries the sense of things fully carried out and completed. It is a word of settled accomplishment. The things he writes about are not hopes or rumours but events that have come to their intended end.

His titles for the earlier tradition are carefully paired: 'eyewitnesses' and 'servants of the word,' verse 2. The first term, autoptai, means those who saw with their own eyes. The second means those who then served the word, the ones who ministered what they had seen. Together they describe a chain from observation to proclamation, and Luke places himself as the one who has investigated it all, verse 3. The adjective 'most excellent,' kratiste, is the one used of the governors Felix and Festus in Acts 23:26 and 24:3, which suggests rank.

The description of Zechariah and Elizabeth is in the language of the law. They are 'righteous,' dikaioi, in the sight of God, and walk 'blamelessly,' amemptoi, in all the commandments and decrees of the Lord, verse 6. The same adjective, amemptos, is used by Paul of his former life under the law, Philippians 3:6. The word describes irreproachable conduct before the community, and Luke uses it here to establish that their suffering is not punishment.

The names themselves are small sermons. Zechariah means 'the LORD remembers,' and John means 'the LORD is gracious,' and the whole passage is about a God who remembers and shows grace. The angel says the name is to be given, verse 13, and when the neighbours want the child named after his father, Elizabeth says, 'He shall be called John,' verse 60.

Gabriel's description of John's task uses three verbs. He will 'turn back,' epistrepho, many of Israel to the Lord, verse 16, the standard verb of repentance. He will 'make ready,' hetoimazo, a people, and that people is 'prepared,' kataskeuazo, for the Lord, verse 17. The pairing means that John's work is to get a people into a condition fit for the Lord's arrival, not simply to announce His coming.

Elizabeth's word for 'disgrace,' oneidos, verse 25, is the word the Greek Old Testament uses in Rachel's mouth: 'God has taken away my shame,' Genesis 30:23. Luke places Elizabeth beside Rachel.

The silence of Zechariah is described in two ways. Gabriel says he will be silent and unable to speak, verse 20. When he comes out, the narrator says he 'remained speechless,' verse 22, a word that can mean mute or deaf. When the neighbours later 'made signs to his father,' verse 62, as though he could not hear, some think his deafness was part of the sign. Luke does not say, and the point is that the silence lasted until the child was named.

typology.fulfillment: Sarah, Rachel and Hannah were each given a child by God after long barrenness, and each child carried the story forward: Isaac, Joseph, Samuel. Manoah's wife, in Judges 13:2-5, bore Samson, who was to begin the deliverance of Israel. Elizabeth is placed in this line, and her son is greater than any of them as a forerunner. What is only a pattern in the earlier stories, God giving life where there was none, becomes the opening of the story of the Messiah. The type falls short in that none of those sons could save; John himself points away from himself to the One who does.

Malachi promised that Elijah would be sent 'before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD,' Malachi 4:5. Gabriel announces that John will go before the Lord 'in the spirit and power of Elijah,' verse 17. Like Elijah, John is a prophet in the wilderness who confronts a king and calls the people back, 1 Kings 18:21. In Jesus' own words the pattern is fulfilled in John, Matthew 11:14. The escalation is that Elijah prepared for a day of judgment, while John prepares the way for a Lord who will come to His people. John also falls short of Elijah's miracles, and he points forward to One who will do more.

typology.type: The priest in the temple and the Lord who comes to His temple
typology.fulfillment: Zechariah offers incense in the Holy Place while the people pray outside, the picture of Israel's worship at its most solemn. Malachi had said 'the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to His temple,' Malachi 3:1. The angel stands at the altar of incense and announces that the one who will prepare the way is coming. In the next chapter the child Jesus is brought to this temple, Luke 2:22-38, and later He teaches in it. The old system of priest, incense and prayer from outside meets the One who will make it unnecessary, as Hebrews describes, Hebrews 9:11-12. The type is partial, since a priest who comes out unable to speak cannot bless the people, and the old order is left speechless.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ by preparation, which is the passage's whole business. The angel's description of John is a description of the one John serves. John will 'go on before the Lord,' verse 17, and the great hope of the Old Testament was that the LORD Himself would come. Isaiah's voice cries, 'Prepare the way for the LORD,' Isaiah 40:3, and Luke later applies that text to John, Luke 3:4. In the next scene Elizabeth calls Mary 'the mother of my Lord,' 1:43. The reader is being asked to see that the Lord whose way John prepares is the child to be born in Nazareth. That is a remarkable claim, because it fits Jesus into the place that Isaiah and Malachi reserved for God Himself.

It leads to Christ by contrast. John is 'great in the sight of the Lord,' verse 15, but the greatness of Jesus, announced in verse 32, is of another order. John will be filled with the Spirit from the womb; Jesus will be conceived by the Spirit. John turns people back to the Lord; Jesus is the Lord. The Gospel of John makes the same point in its own words: 'He himself was not the Light, but he came to testify about the Light,' John 1:8. Luke prepares the whole Gospel to be about the Light by first showing the one who is not.

It leads to Christ by promise kept. Gabriel's mention of the spirit of Elijah, of turning hearts, and of a prepared people ties the opening of Luke to Malachi, and so says that what Malachi wrote has begun to happen. When Zechariah's mouth is opened he praises God for 'a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David,' 1:69, and says that his own son 'will go on before the Lord to prepare the way for Him,' 1:76. The child in Elizabeth's womb is the herald of the child who will be the horn.

It leads to Christ by joy. The word 'joy' occurs in the angel's promise, verse 14, and in the neighbours' joy at the birth, verse 58. The gospel that Luke will tell is good news, euangelizo, verse 19, and Gabriel is the first herald of it. The whole Gospel is to be a story of rejoicing, and its first note is that one barren woman has been remembered.

A word of care: Zechariah and Elizabeth are not allegories. The temple, the incense and the barren womb are real things that happened, and the connections to Christ come from how Luke and the New Testament use them, not from reading every detail as a code. What the chapter gives us is the first movement of a long preparation, and Luke's own record, Luke 24:25-27, says the whole of Scripture leads to the Christ who suffered and entered His glory.
study.god:
The passage shows a God who hears. Gabriel says, 'your prayer has been heard,' verse 13, and the verb tells us the answer is a response to a specific longing. A man and woman had prayed through decades, and in their old age God answers. The God of Luke 1 is not the God who forgets the quiet. He is attentive to those that the world overlooks, and He is faithful over a long time.

He is a God of promise and of timing. The angel says the words 'will be fulfilled at their proper time,' verse 20. God's timing is not hurried and not late. The four hundred years since Malachi may have felt like silence, but the narrative treats them as preparation. God was not absent from them, and the moment He chooses to act is exact. Paul would later say 'when the time had fully come, God sent His Son,' Galatians 4:4.

He is holy and approachable at once. Gabriel stands 'in the presence of God,' verse 19, and the priest in the temple is gripped with fear. God is not casual, and His messenger's first words are 'Do not be afraid.' The temple setting, with its altar and incense, reminds us that God is to be approached on His terms. Yet the message He sends is of joy and favour.

He is the God who works through weakness. He does not need youth, strength or position. He takes an old priest and a woman long thought barren, and as Gabriel will tell Mary, 'no word from God will ever fail,' Luke 1:37. Whatever He intends, He is able to do. This is the same God who asked Abraham, 'Is anything too difficult for the LORD?' Genesis 18:14.

He is just as well as gracious. Zechariah's silence is real, a consequence of unbelief. God does not pretend that doubt is nothing. Yet the discipline is limited, tied to a day, and wrapped in a promise that will come to pass. It is a picture of God's way of correcting those He loves.

He is the God who sends the Spirit. John will be 'filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb,' verse 15. Luke's Gospel and Acts are full of the Spirit, and the first mention is here. The God of Israel is not remote; His Spirit is already at work before the child is born.

For worship, the passage invites us to wait with trust. Zechariah and Elizabeth were righteous before they were rewarded, and the word of promise came in the middle of ordinary duty. We are asked to keep walking in the commandments, to keep praying, and to believe that the God who has heard will answer at His time, and in a way larger than we asked.

crossReferences.note: 'I will send My messenger, who will prepare the way before Me.' This is the promise Luke 1:17 and 1:76 take up for John. The messenger prepares the way before the LORD, and the LORD then 'will suddenly come to His temple.' Luke begins in that very temple, with the messenger's father.

The last words of the Old Testament promise Elijah before the great day of the LORD, who will turn the hearts of fathers and children. Gabriel quotes this almost directly in Luke 1:17. After four hundred years the final promise of the Old Testament begins to be kept.

Abraham and Sarah were old, and Sarah laughed. The answer is the question Luke's whole chapter echoes: 'Is anything too difficult for the LORD?' Zechariah has the same history to remember and yet asks for a sign. The comparison shows how much he should have trusted.

Hannah prayed for a son, and 'the LORD remembered her.' Samuel became the prophet who anointed the kings of Israel. Zechariah's name means that the LORD remembers, and Elizabeth's story parallels Hannah's to show that God's remembering is a saving act.

The angel of the LORD told Manoah's barren wife to avoid wine and strong drink and promised a son who would begin Israel's deliverance. Luke 1:15 uses the same language for John: he will never take wine or strong drink. It marks him as set apart for God from the womb.

Gabriel came to Daniel 'about the time of the evening sacrifice' with an answer that had gone out 'at the beginning of your petitions.' Gabriel again appears at the hour of incense with an answer to prayer. The setting recalls Daniel's long waiting for restoration.

'Prepare the way for the LORD in the wilderness.' Luke 3:4-6 quotes this of John, and Luke 1:76 anticipates it. The voice in the wilderness prepares not just for a prophet or a king but for the LORD Himself, and the glory of the LORD 'will be revealed.'

After his silence ends, Zechariah is filled with the Holy Spirit and sings of a horn of salvation in David's house, of the oath to Abraham, and of his own son who will go before the Lord. It is the answer to his doubt in verse 18, and it interprets the whole chapter.

Jesus says no one born of women is greater than John, and that 'he is the Elijah who was to come.' This confirms Gabriel's words and sets the limit on John's greatness: he is the last of the old order, and the least in the kingdom stands in something greater.

'He himself was not the Light, but he came to testify about the Light.' John's Gospel puts the same truth briefly: the forerunner is a witness, not the one to whom witness is borne. It is the neat summary of the child announced in Luke 1:13-17.

Luke's second volume begins, 'In my first book, O Theophilus,' and speaks of 'all that Jesus began to do and to teach.' It ties the preface of Luke 1:1-4 to the whole two part work, and shows the purpose of certainty is meant to cover the life of Jesus and the work of the church.

'God remembered Rachel. He listened to her and opened her womb... God has taken away my shame.' Elizabeth's words in Luke 1:25 are close to Rachel's, and the Greek Old Testament uses the same word for shame. The barrenness of the matriarchs is the model for her story.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story came to a pause at the end of the Old Testament. Malachi ended with a promise and a warning, that Elijah would come and turn hearts or God would strike the land with a curse, Malachi 4:5-6. Between that last page and Luke's first lie roughly four centuries in which Israel had returned from exile, rebuilt a temple, and still lived under foreign rule. The long question was whether the promises made to Abraham, to David and through the prophets had been forgotten.

Luke 1 answers by returning to the pattern that began with Abraham and Sarah. When God started His rescue of the world, He did it through a childless old couple, and now He starts the next stage the same way. The God who made a nation out of one barren woman is making the way for a Saviour out of another. Behind the pattern is Genesis 3:15, the promise that a seed of the woman would crush the serpent. Each birth in the line of barrenness kept that promise alive, and Luke is bringing the line to its end.

Luke 1 also begins a theme that runs through both of his volumes: that the word of God is certain and moves forward in history. The prologue says that these matters have been 'fulfilled,' and the book is built to show how. The temple will be the first scene; it will be where Jesus teaches in His last week, and where the first church gathers in Acts. The priest who comes out speechless is a sign that the old order has reached the limit of its ability to speak, and a new word is coming.

The story's end is the one the forerunner pointed to. John prepared a people for the Lord, and Luke's Gospel ends with that people sent out in the Lord's name, Luke 24:47. The final book of the Bible shows the people prepared at last, with all things made new and God dwelling with them, Revelation 21:3-5. Everything Luke 1 starts is finished there: the barren are remembered, the humble are lifted, and the Lord who was announced in a temple dwells with His people for ever.

sermon.title: Elizabeth and Zechariah
sermon.why: From Begg's series on Luke's infancy narratives, this message expounds Luke 1:5-23, the account of the aged, childless priest and his wife and the promise of John, showing how God works amazing things in the midst of ordinary, faithful lives. A careful, expository handling of this movement.

quiz.q: Why does Luke say he wrote his Gospel?

options.text: So that Theophilus may know the certainty of the things he has been taught.
options.note: Luke states this purpose plainly in verse 4: assurance grounded in a careful account.

options.text: To give an orderly, carefully investigated account of what was fulfilled.
options.note: True, and Luke says this, but the account serves the deeper goal of the reader's certainty.

options.text: To record his own personal opinions about Jesus.
options.note: Luke relies on eyewitnesses and careful investigation, not mere opinion.

options.text: To entertain readers with religious legends.
options.note: Luke writes verifiable history for assurance, the opposite of legend.

quiz.q: What did the angel Gabriel tell Zechariah?

options.text: His prayer was heard, and Elizabeth would bear a son, John, who would go before the Lord in the spirit of Elijah.
options.note: This is the heart of Gabriel's message in verses 13 to 17.

options.text: Elizabeth would have a son who would bring him great joy.
options.note: True, but it leaves out John's central mission to prepare a people for the Lord.

options.text: Zechariah himself would become a great prophet.
options.note: The promise concerned his son John, not Zechariah's own prophetic career.

options.text: He should stop praying because God would not answer.
options.note: The opposite: God had heard and was answering his prayer.

quiz.q: Why was Zechariah unable to speak?

options.text: Because he did not believe Gabriel's words, so he was silent until they were fulfilled.
options.note: Gabriel gives this reason directly in verse 20.

options.text: Because he had seen a vision in the temple and was overwhelmed.
options.note: The people guessed this, but the stated cause was his unbelief.

options.text: Because it was the custom for priests to keep silence after serving.
options.note: There was no such custom; the silence was a specific sign to Zechariah.

options.text: Because Elizabeth had asked him not to tell anyone.
options.note: The silence came from Gabriel's word, not from Elizabeth.

quiz.q: In whose spirit and power would John come?

options.text: In the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn hearts and make ready a people for the Lord.
options.note: Verse 17 names Elijah, fulfilling Malachi's promise.

options.text: In the power of the Holy Spirit, with whom he was filled from the womb.
options.note: True and stated in verse 15, but the specific comparison in verse 17 is to Elijah.

options.text: In the spirit of Moses the lawgiver.
options.note: The text points to Elijah, the promised forerunner, not Moses.

options.text: In his own strength and eloquence.
options.note: John's power was from God, not himself.

quiz.q: How did Elizabeth respond when she conceived?

options.text: She rejoiced that the Lord had shown her favor and taken away her disgrace.
options.note: Her words in verse 25 give thanks to God for removing her reproach.

options.text: She kept to herself in seclusion for five months.
options.note: True, she did remain in seclusion, but her heart's response was thankful joy in God.

options.text: She doubted the pregnancy could be real.
options.note: It was Zechariah who doubted; Elizabeth praised God.

options.text: She complained that it had come too late in life.
options.note: She gave thanks, not complaint, for God's kindness.

questions: Luke wrote so that his reader might know the certainty of the gospel. Where do you long for more assurance, and how might a careful look at the Scriptures steady your faith?
God broke centuries of silence to answer the prayers of an ordinary couple. Have you grown weary in a prayer you have prayed for years, and what would it mean to keep bringing it to God?
Zechariah and Elizabeth were righteous, yet they still carried a deep disappointment. How do you hold together faithfulness to God and the ache of unanswered longing?
Zechariah doubted and was disciplined, yet God still kept His promise. How does it comfort you that God's purposes do not depend on the strength of your faith?
John's whole calling was to point away from himself to the Lord. In what ways is God calling you to prepare the way for others to see Jesus?

translationNotes.note: The sentence here quotes Malachi 4:5-6, building to the clause to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.
Orderly account renders a Greek word meaning in sequence or in an arranged order; Luke claims a coherent, well-ordered telling, not merely a strict calendar of events.
Filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb marks John as set apart by God before birth, echoing the language of Nazirite dedication and the calling of prophets like Samuel and Jeremiah.
